relationship: The Creator endures beyond the created world
rationale: Psalm89 places God's existence before mountains and the formed world. Psalm101 contrasts the founded earth and heavens, which will perish, with the Lord who remains and whose years do not fail. The creation and divine-duration contrast is explicit in both.

relationship: Blossoming and vanishing life as grass
rationale: Psalm89 pictures morning blossoming followed by evening drying. Psalm102 likens human days to grass and a field flower, followed by a passing wind and disappearance. Both develop the short course of flourishing vegetation as an image of mortality, with different descriptions of its passing.

relationship: Morning mercy accompanied by exultation
rationale: Psalm89 reports being filled with God's mercy in the morning and rejoicing. Psalm58 resolves to exult in His mercy in the morning. The distinctive morning-mercy-and-joy combination corresponds, while the reported past and prospective resolve remain different.

relationship: Dwelling within God's protective shelter
rationale: Psalm90 joins dwelling in the Most High's help with lodging in divine shelter. Psalm26 describes being hidden and sheltered in God's tent during trouble. Both portray divine protection through a sheltered dwelling, without identifying the psalm's lodging with a particular physical tent.

relationship: God as helper, refuge and object of hope
rationale: The confession in Psalm90 combines my Helper, my refuge, my God and hope in Him. Psalm17 combines refuge, rescuer, my God, helper and hope in Him in its longer list of protective titles. The cluster of titles and hope formula supplies the correspondence.

relationship: Rescue from the hunters' trap
rationale: Psalm90 promises rescue from the hunters' trap. Psalm123 pictures the rescued community's soul as a bird escaping a shattered hunters' trap. The trap and rescue correspond; the bird and broken-trap details belong to the target.

relationship: Protection pictured beneath God's wings
rationale: Psalm90 promises overshadowing and hope beneath divine wings. Psalm16 asks to be guarded and says God will shelter the speaker in the shelter of His wings. Both use the wing-shelter image, while the request and assurances retain their distinct forms.

relationship: Fearless rest and approaching threats
rationale: Psalm90 speaks of freedom from night terror and the day's missile. Proverbs promises pleasant sleep and freedom from approaching fright or ungodly assault under the Lord's support. The comparison joins protected rest with threatened attack; the target does not supply the missile image.

relationship: Seeing the outcome of sinners' wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm90 says the protected person will observe sinners' repayment with his eyes. Psalm36 says the one waiting for the Lord will see when sinners are destroyed. Both expressly describe witnessing judgment; the target additionally speaks of inheriting the land.

relationship: Same-chapter return to refuge and hope
rationale: After the descriptions of danger, verse9 returns to the opening Most High, refuge and hope vocabulary. This repeated confession links the opening shelter statement to the ensuing protection promises. The verse's changes of address are preserved without assigning every pronoun an inferred speaker.

relationship: Knowing God's name and hoping in Him
rationale: Psalm90 joins the protected person's hope with knowing God's name. Psalm9 calls those who know His name to hope in Him and says He has not abandoned His seekers. The shared knowing-name and hope combination is more specific than a general rescue theme.

relationship: Calling in affliction and receiving rescue
rationale: Both join calling upon God in affliction with His rescue. Their final glorifying clauses differ: Psalm90 has God glorify the rescued person, while Psalm49 has the rescued person glorify God. The correspondence preserves that reversal of agency.

relationship: Length of days granted by God
rationale: Psalm90 promises to fill the protected person with length of days. Psalm20 reports the king asking God for life and receiving length of days. Both explicitly present prolonged life as divinely given, with different beneficiaries and forms of speech.

relationship: Thanksgiving and music to the name of the Most High
rationale: Psalm91 joins thanks to the Lord with music to the name of the Most High. Psalm7 likewise joins thanks to the Lord with singing praise to the name of the Lord Most High. The combined acts and divine title form a close verbal parallel.

relationship: Declaring morning mercy after experiencing it
rationale: Psalm91 makes declaring divine mercy in the morning part of its thanksgiving. Psalm89 reports being filled with that mercy in the morning and rejoicing. The morning-mercy wording corresponds, while Psalm91 adds its distinct declaration of truth by night.

relationship: Rejoicing in God's works with different celebrants
rationale: Psalm91 says God's making gladdened the speaker, who will exult at His handiwork. Psalm103 says the Lord will rejoice in His works. The shared joy-in-divine-works pattern preserves the difference between the human celebrant and God Himself.

relationship: The depth of divine thought and wisdom
rationale: The psalm calls God's reasonings very deep. Romans praises the depth of His wisdom and knowledge and asks who knew His mind. Both portray divine understanding through depth and limited human comprehension, without treating the passages as identical quotations.

relationship: Lawless flourishing pictured as short-lived grass
rationale: Psalm91 pictures sinners springing up like grass before destruction. Psalm36 warns against envying evildoers because they will dry up like grass and fall like green plants. The same vegetation image interprets the apparent flourishing of the lawless.

relationship: The scattering of God's opponents
rationale: Psalm91 predicts the perishing of God's enemies and the scattering of workers of lawlessness. Psalm67 asks that God arise and His enemies be scattered. The dispersal language corresponds while each verse's subjects and prediction or petition remain intact.

relationship: The raised horn as a personal image of strength
rationale: Psalm91 says the speaker's horn will be raised like a one-horned creature's. Hannah's song says her horn is exalted in her God. The personal horn-exaltation metaphor corresponds; the psalm's animal comparison and old-age-in-oil clause are not supplied to Hannah's words.

relationship: The righteous person as a flourishing tree
rationale: Psalm91 compares the righteous to a blossoming palm and a multiplying cedar of Lebanon. Psalm1 depicts the person who delights in the law as a planted, fruitful tree. Both portray righteous life through sustained tree growth, with distinct species and settings.

relationship: A fruitful tree within God's house
rationale: Psalm91 places the flourishing trees in the Lord's house and courts. Psalm51 compares the speaker to a fruitful olive tree in God's house. The shared divine-house and fruitful-tree combination is explicit, while the olive remains distinct from the preceding palm and cedar.

relationship: A favorable old age associated with righteousness
rationale: Within its portrait of the righteous, Psalm91 describes multiplying and flourishing in a rich old age. Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in ways of righteousness. Both give a positive image of age in relation to righteous living, without equating their tree and crown metaphors.

relationship: God's righteousness excludes injustice
rationale: Psalm91 declares the Lord upright with no injustice in Him. Deuteronomy calls Him faithful, without unrighteousness, righteous and holy. The explicit denial of injustice alongside divine righteousness forms the comparison.

relationship: Divine kingship and the unshaken world
rationale: Both announce the Lord's reign and connect it with His establishing the inhabited world so that it will not be shaken. Psalm92 adds clothing and girding with power; Psalm95 adds the announcement among nations and upright judgment.

relationship: The enduring divine throne
rationale: Psalm92 joins the throne's readiness from then with God's existence from the age. Lamentations confesses that the Lord will dwell for ever and His throne endures through generations. Both affirm divine rule's duration amid otherwise different poetic settings.

relationship: Rivers personified with voices and hands
rationale: Psalm92 pictures rivers lifting their voices. Psalm97 pictures rivers clapping their hands as mountains exult. Both give rivers human expressive action in proclamations of the Lord's rule, one vocal and the other applause; the source's emotion is not otherwise specified.

relationship: Many waters in a portrayal of divine majesty
rationale: Psalm92 speaks of the voices of many waters, wondrous sea surges and the Lord wondrous on high. Psalm28 describes the Lord's voice over waters and the Lord over many waters. The audible waters and divine majesty correspond without making the waters' voices identical to God's voice.

relationship: Vengeance belongs to the Lord
rationale: Psalm93 calls the Lord the God of vengeance. Romans forbids private vengeance and cites the Lord's claim that vengeance and repayment are His. The divine ownership of vengeance connects the texts; Paul's corresponding instruction to believers is stated in its own context.

relationship: Appeal to the Judge of all the earth
rationale: Psalm93 invokes the Judge of the earth to repay the arrogant. Abraham appeals to the One judging all the earth to do justice in distinguishing righteous and ungodly. Both appeal to God's universal judicial authority, while requesting different judicial outcomes.

relationship: Questioning the boasting of wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm93 asks how long sinners will boast. Psalm51 asks why the mighty one boasts in wickedness and lawlessness. Both make wrongful boasting the object of a direct rhetorical challenge, without identifying the psalm's sinners with the person addressed in Psalm51.

relationship: Oppression of God's people and inheritance
rationale: Psalm93 says opponents humbled God's people and mistreated His inheritance. Isaiah addresses the daughter of the Chaldeans for defiling His inheritance and showing His people no mercy. The paired people-and-inheritance description and oppressive treatment correspond without identifying the unnamed opponents.

relationship: Wrongdoers claim the Lord does not see
rationale: Psalm93 reports the claim that the Lord will not see or understand. Ezekiel reports elders acting secretly and saying the Lord does not see and has abandoned the land. The explicit denial of divine sight corresponds, without equating the two groups or their acts.

relationship: A beatitude for the person God disciplines
rationale: The psalm calls happy the person the Lord disciplines and teaches. Eliphaz likewise calls happy the person the Lord reproved. This is a comparison of their beatitude wording, not an endorsement of Eliphaz's application to Job; the friends' speech is qualified by the reproof in Job42:7-8.

relationship: Divine rescue and the soul's relation to Hades
rationale: Psalm93 says that without the Lord's help the speaker's soul would almost have sojourned in Hades. Psalm29 thanks the Lord for bringing his soul up from Hades. Both use the soul-and-Hades image for mortal danger and divine rescue, in counterfactual and retrospective forms.

relationship: The confession of an unsteady foot
rationale: Psalm93 joins saying that the foot has been shaken with the Lord's helping mercy. Psalm72 confesses that the feet were almost shaken while envying sinners' peace. The personal foot-instability image corresponds, while the target expressly supplies its own occasion of envy.

relationship: Authority that produces oppressive ordinances
rationale: The psalm questions whether a throne of lawlessness shaping toil by command can join God. Isaiah condemns writers of wickedness who turn aside the poor's judgment and exploit widows and orphans. Both expose official command or writing used as an instrument of injustice.

relationship: Collective plotting against righteous life
rationale: Psalm93 describes hunting a righteous person's soul and condemning innocent blood. Proverbs exposes a group's invitation to bloodshed and to hiding a righteous man unjustly in the earth. The shared targeting of righteous life is retained, with judicial condemnation and the criminal invitation distinguished.

relationship: The refuge, helper and hope confession repeated
rationale: Psalm93 joins the Lord as refuge with God as helper of the speaker's hope. Psalm90 combines my Helper, my refuge, my God and hope in Him. The repeated cluster of protective titles supplies the correspondence while preserving the different construction of hope.

relationship: Repayment measured by wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm93 predicts repayment of lawlessness according to wickedness. Psalm27 petitions for repayment according to opponents' works and the wickedness of their practices. The parallel joins repayment, wrongdoing and the according-to formulation, while prediction and request remain distinct.

relationship: Paired calls to exult and raise a shout
rationale: Psalm94 calls the community to exult in the Lord and shout to God its Savior. Psalm80 pairs exultation in God its helper with a shout to the God of Jacob. The paired acclamations correspond without equating their distinct headings or festival contexts.

relationship: Approaching God with thanksgiving and psalms
rationale: Psalm94 calls for coming before God's face with thanksgiving and psalms. Psalm99 calls for entering His gates with thanksgiving and courts with hymns. The shared approach-plus-thanksgiving-and-music pattern is explicit, with different descriptions of the place of approach.

relationship: Divine greatness above all gods
rationale: Psalm94 calls the Lord a great God and great King above all gods. Psalm95 likewise declares the Lord great and fearsome above all gods. The closely repeated greatness-and-above-all-gods formula receives a royal designation in Psalm94 and a fearsome designation in Psalm95.

relationship: The earth and mountains in God's hand
rationale: The psalm places earth's ends in God's hand and assigns Him the mountain heights. Isaiah asks who measured earth with a handful and weighed the mountains. Both express divine command of immense landforms through the hand and measures, with possession and measuring distinguished.

relationship: Forty years of wilderness judgment
rationale: The psalm remembers forty years of divine vexation with the wandering generation. Numbers announces forty years in the wilderness bearing sins and knowing God's anger. The stated duration, wilderness generation and divine anger provide the narrative correspondence without making every clause an exact quotation.

relationship: Honor before God and qualities of His holy place
rationale: Both arrange qualities before God and qualities in His place. The psalm gives thanksgiving and beauty, then holiness and magnificence in His sanctuary; Chronicles gives glory and praise, then strength and boasting in His place. The parallel structure preserves these lexical differences.

relationship: Islands included in worldwide rejoicing and praise
rationale: Psalm96 calls the earth and many islands to rejoice at the Lord's kingship. Isaiah's new hymn addresses the earth's extremity and island inhabitants and announces praise in the islands. Both expressly extend the celebration to islands, without assigning the psalm's land-establishment heading a historical event.

relationship: Righteousness and judgment establish the divine throne
rationale: Both place righteousness and judgment in the establishment or preparation of God's throne. Psalm96 surrounds Him with cloud and gloom; Psalm88 has mercy and truth go before His face. The shared throne formula is distinguished from their surrounding imagery.

relationship: Fire preceding the divine approach
rationale: Psalm96 describes fire going before God and burning His enemies. Psalm49 describes God coming manifestly with fire burning before Him and a surrounding tempest. Both place fire before the approaching God, with different descriptions of its surroundings and effects.

relationship: World-illuminating lightning and the shaken earth
rationale: Both say divine lightning shone upon the inhabited world and that the earth shook. Psalm76 additionally describes the voice of thunder in the wheel. The lightning-and-earth response is a close verbal parallel, with that additional image left in the target.

relationship: The heavens announce God's righteousness
rationale: Both expressly give the heavens the action of announcing God's righteousness. Psalm49 connects this with God as judge; Psalm96 joins it to all peoples seeing His glory. The shared announcement clause retains its different neighboring explanations.

relationship: Zion and Judea's daughters rejoice at God's judgments
rationale: Both join Zion's rejoicing with the exultation of Judea's daughters because of the Lord's judgments. Psalm96 reports that Zion heard and rejoiced; Psalm47 frames the shared response as a summons. The location, participants and reason all correspond.

relationship: The Most High over all the earth
rationale: Both identify the Lord as Most High over all the earth. Psalm96 adds His exaltation above all gods, while Psalm82 asks opponents to recognize His name and unique height. The shared worldwide Most High formula is explicit.

relationship: Light associated with righteous life
rationale: Psalm96 says light has dawned for the righteous. Proverbs describes righteous ways shining like light and advancing toward the day. Both portray righteous life through illumination, with a light dawning for people distinguished from their ways themselves shining.

relationship: The holy arm and divine salvation
rationale: Psalm97 attributes salvation to God's right hand and holy arm. Isaiah says the Lord will uncover His holy arm before nations and the earth's ends will see salvation from God. The holy-arm and salvation combination is explicit, with achieved salvation and future manifestation distinguished.

relationship: Salvation made visible before the nations
rationale: Psalm97 reports salvation made known and righteousness revealed before the nations. Isaiah promises the unveiling of God's holy arm before all nations and salvation seen at earth's ends. Both present divine rescue publicly to nations; righteousness and the holy arm remain their distinct revealed objects.

relationship: All the earth summoned to shout and make music
rationale: Both address all the earth with a shout to God and an accompanying call to music. Psalm97 adds singing and exultation; Psalm65 specifies music to His name and glory to His praise. The repeated worldwide acclamation-and-music pattern supplies the link.

relationship: Music to God with a lyre
rationale: Psalm97 repeats the lyre in its command to make music to the Lord. Psalm146 likewise commands music to God with a lyre after beginning with thanksgiving. The particular instrument and God-directed musical command correspond without identifying a single performance.

relationship: Hammered trumpets in worship
rationale: The psalm names hammered trumpets in its acclamation before the Lord as King. Numbers orders two silver trumpets made of hammered work, within instructions that include their use at feasts and offerings. The manufacture and instrument type correspond; the psalm's horn trumpet is a separate named instrument.

relationship: The sea and its fullness in the creation summons
rationale: Both call for the sea and all that fills it to be shaken. Psalm97 adds the inhabited world and its dwellers, whereas Psalm95 first calls heaven and earth to rejoice. The closely repeated sea clause links the two creation-wide summonses.

relationship: Clapping nature and rejoicing mountains
rationale: Psalm97 has rivers clap their hands and mountains exult. Isaiah has mountains and hills leap in joy and field trees clap their branches. Both combine joyful mountains with clapping nonhuman creation, preserving rivers versus trees and hands versus branches.

relationship: The repeated closing announcement of world judgment
rationale: Both close their creation rejoicing with the Lord's coming to judge the earth and world in righteousness. Psalm97 says He has come and peoples will be judged with uprightness; Psalm95 says He is coming and gives His truth. The parallel ending preserves tense and final-attribute differences.

relationship: The Lord seated upon the cherubim
rationale: Psalm98 describes the reigning Lord seated upon the cherubim. Samuel uses the same throne description when the Lord's ark is carried from Shiloh. The shared divine title does not identify the psalm with that battle or endorse the Israelites' expectation that bringing the ark guarantees victory.

relationship: The divine name as holy and fearsome
rationale: Psalm98 calls for thanks to the great name because it is fearsome and holy. Psalm110 concludes its redemption-and-covenant statement by calling His name holy and fearsome. The paired attributes explicitly qualify the divine name in both.

relationship: Royal authority prepared with righteousness
rationale: Psalm98 says the King's honor loves judgment and that God prepared uprightness. Proverbs says a ruling throne is prepared with righteousness and evil is abhorrent to a king. Both connect royal authority, moral judgment and prepared righteousness, while God's action and the human royal maxim remain distinct.

relationship: Bowing toward the place of God's feet
rationale: Psalm98 commands bowing at God's footstool. Psalm131 resolves to enter His dwellings and bow toward the place where His feet stood. The low place associated with divine feet and the act of bowing correspond; no independent object identity is asserted for the footstool.

relationship: Samuel calls upon the Lord and is heard
rationale: The psalm names Samuel among those who called on God and were heard. Samuel narrates Israel requesting his intercession, his cry for Israel and the Lord hearing him. The named person and call-and-hearing action provide the concrete narrative link; the psalm also names Moses and Aaron.

relationship: Same-chapter framing by exaltation and bowing
rationale: Verses5 and9 repeat Exalt the Lord our God, the call to bow, and the reason of holiness. Footstool and holy mountain give the two locations. The refrain frames the intervening account of mediators calling upon God and His answer and judgment.

relationship: The all-earth acclamation repeated
rationale: Psalm99 opens its thanksgiving with the command that all the earth shout to the Lord. Psalm97 uses the same all-earth shout to God before further musical commands. The concise worldwide acclamation formula links these neighboring praise psalms.

relationship: Serving the Lord with gladness
rationale: Psalm99 commands service to the Lord with gladness. Deuteronomy identifies failure to serve Him with gladness and a good heart as grounds for the ensuing judgment. The same service-and-gladness combination appears as positive summons and reproach for its absence.

relationship: The Creator's people and the sheep of His pasture
rationale: Psalm99 joins God's making us with His people and the sheep of His pasture. Psalm94 likewise joins the Lord who made us with our God, the people of His pasture and sheep of His hand. The combined creation-and-flock confession corresponds, including the differing hand clause.

relationship: Entering the Lord's gates with thanksgiving
rationale: Psalm99 commands entry through God's gates with thanksgiving. Psalm117 requests the opening of righteousness's gates and says the entrant will thank the Lord, then names the Lord's gate. The gate, entry and thanksgiving sequence is explicit in both.

relationship: Enduring mercy and truth in praise
rationale: Psalm99 joins everlasting mercy with truth through generations. Psalm116 joins mercy grown strong over the people with the Lord's truth remaining for ever. Both pair mercy and truth in praise; the duration clauses are retained with the attributes to which each text attaches them.

relationship: Mercy and judgment paired
rationale: The speaker will sing mercy and judgment to the Lord. Psalm32 explicitly says God loves mercy and judgment. The same ethical pair is the song's subject in one passage and the object of divine love in the other.

relationship: Personal refusal of company with wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm100 says the speaker did not set a lawless matter before his eyes and hated transgressors. Psalm25 says he did not sit with emptiness and hated an assembly of evildoers. The paired avowal of refusal and hatred corresponds while their specified acts remain different.

relationship: Speech against the neighbor excluded
rationale: Psalm100 reports driving away one speaking secretly against his neighbor. Psalm14's qualified dweller does not act deceitfully with his tongue or take up reproach against those nearest him. Both exclude damaging neighbor-directed speech from accepted conduct, with their different actions and agents preserved.

relationship: Blameless walking as a qualification for dwelling and service
rationale: Psalm100 chooses faithful people to sit with the speaker and the blameless walker to minister to him. Psalm14 asks who may dwell with the Lord and answers with one walking blamelessly. The shared admission criterion is explicit; the speaker's attendants and God's dwelling guests are distinct roles.

relationship: Wrongdoers excluded from dwelling and presence
rationale: Psalm100 says arrogance did not dwell in the speaker's house and unjust speech did not prosper before his eyes. Psalm5 says an evildoer will not sojourn with God and the lawless will not remain before His eyes. The dwelling-and-before-the-eyes pattern is shared, with human household and divine presence distinguished.

relationship: Pouring out a plea in despondency
rationale: The heading describes a poor person becoming despondent and pouring out a petition before the Lord. Psalm141 resolves to pour out a plea before Him and recalls the spirit failing within. The pouring-prayer and inward-collapse combination corresponds without identifying the anonymous sufferer with David's cave setting.

relationship: The face, affliction and swift-hearing plea
rationale: Both ask God not to turn His face away and join affliction with a plea to hear quickly. Psalm101 also asks Him to incline His ear whenever called. The shared sequence of face, affliction and prompt hearing makes the parallel particular.

relationship: Same-chapter recurrence of grass drying up
rationale: The struck and dried heart is likened to grass in verse5; verse12 again says the speaker dried up like grass while describing declining days. The repeated drying-grass simile links bodily affliction with the poem's later statement of temporal frailty.

relationship: Raven imagery in sparsely inhabited places
rationale: The psalm compares the speaker to a wilderness pelican and a night raven on a house site. Isaiah places birds including ravens in land destined for enduring desolation. The avian and deserted-place imagery corresponds; night raven and raven are not asserted to be identical species, nor is the sufferer's situation identified with that judgment.

relationship: Tears incorporated into food and drink imagery
rationale: Psalm101 reports ashes eaten like bread and drink mixed with weeping. Psalm79 asks whether God will feed bread of tears and give tears to drink by measure. Both combine bread, drink and grief, with ashes and the measure kept in their respective texts.

relationship: Being cast down after elevation
rationale: The afflicted speaker says God lifted him and then dashed him down. Psalm72 describes God casting down deceitful people when they were lifted up. The vertical reversal corresponds; comparison of the image does not assign the target's moral characterization of the wicked to the source's complainant.

relationship: Renewed compassion for Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Psalm101 announces that the time for compassion on Zion has come. Zechariah moves from asking how long Jerusalem will lack mercy to God's promise to return in compassion and again have mercy on Zion. The city-specific change from withholding to compassion corresponds without assigning the psalm Zechariah's stated year.

relationship: Concern for the material remains of Jerusalem
rationale: The psalm says God's servants delight in Zion's stones and will have compassion on her dust. Nehemiah grieves over the desolated ancestral city and asks to rebuild it. Both express attachment to the damaged city, while stones and dust and the narrative's tombs and burned gates remain different details.

relationship: All earth's kings respond to the Lord's glory
rationale: Psalm101 anticipates nations fearing the Lord's name and all earth's kings His glory. Psalm137 summons all earth's kings to thanksgiving and song because His glory is great. The worldwide royal response to glory corresponds, while fear and thanksgiving are distinct responses.

relationship: The Lord builds Zion or Jerusalem
rationale: Psalm101 says the Lord will build Zion; Psalm146 says the Lord builds Jerusalem and will gather Israel's dispersed. The divine builder and the holy city correspond. The source additionally describes His appearing in glory rather than the target's gathering clause.

relationship: God hears the lowly and does not disregard them
rationale: Psalm101 pairs regard for the lowly's prayer with not treating their petition as nothing. Psalm68 pairs hearing the needy with not despising His bound ones. The paired divine attention and refusal of disregard correspond, with lowly petitioners, needy people and bound ones kept as each passage names them.

relationship: Divine acts transmitted to a future generation
rationale: The psalm commands a written record for another generation and says the people being created will praise. Psalm77 transmits divine works to sons yet to be born so they may hope in God. Both address a future audience, with writing and repeated telling, and created people and future sons, distinguished.

relationship: Looking from the holy heavenly dwelling
rationale: Psalm101 says the Lord looked from His holy height and from heaven upon earth. Deuteronomy petitions Him to look from His holy house, from heaven, and bless Israel and the land. The holy heavenly vantage and downward attention correspond, in report and petition respectively.

relationship: Hearing those in bonds and preserving the condemned one's sons
rationale: Psalm101 joins hearing the groaning of those in bonds with releasing sons of those put to death. Psalm78 asks that the same groaning enter God's presence and that He preserve sons of those put to death. The two-part formulation is close; the sons are not replaced with people merely sentenced to death.

relationship: The Lord's name proclaimed in Zion's praise
rationale: Psalm101 states the purpose of announcing the Lord's name in Zion and His praise in Jerusalem. Isaiah calls for His name and deeds to be proclaimed and for Zion's inhabitants to rejoice. The name-proclamation and Zion-praise combination corresponds without identifying a single occasion.

relationship: Asking to know the brief measure of one's days
rationale: The psalm's direct speech asks to be told the fewness of my days. Psalm38 asks God to make known life's limit and number of days. The requests concerning life's measure correspond; the source's opening he and him are not assigned unexpressed identities.

relationship: The fear of losing the remaining span of life
rationale: Psalm101 asks not to be taken up at the halfway point of the speaker's days. Hezekiah's prayer speaks of leaving remaining years behind at the height of his days and Hades' gates. The untimely interruption of life corresponds without identifying the psalm's sufferer as Hezekiah.

relationship: Servants' offspring dwelling in restored Zion
rationale: Psalm101 ends with servants' children dwelling and their offspring established for ever. Psalm68 joins God's saving Zion and rebuilding Judea's cities with His servants' offspring possessing it and lovers of His name dwelling there. The restoration, servants' offspring and continuing dwelling cluster corresponds.
